articles.title: In 2002, South Australia sank ex-HMAS Hobart in under 3 minutes; 18 years later, a marine survey recorded more than 50 fish species around the destroyer
articles.summary: Science News: A 134-metre decommissioned guided-missile destroyer lying 30 metres below the surface of Yankalilla Bay has become one of South Australia’s most diver.
articles.body: A 134-metre decommissioned guided-missile destroyer lying 30 metres below the surface of Yankalilla Bay has become one of South Australia’s most diverse marine habitats, less than two decades after it was deliberately sunk. The ex-HMAS Hobart was scuttled on 5 November 2002. It sank in two minutes and 17 seconds after controlled explosives were detonated along its hull, according to the Naval Historical Society of Australia. A detailed scientific survey carried out 18 years after the sinking found that the artificial reef was home to more than 50 different fish species, along with large communities of filter-feeding marine organisms. The findings, published in reports by South Australia’s Department for Environment and Water (DEW), show how old military vessels can be reused to support marine life along areas of sea floor with few natural habitats.Transformation from naval flagship to ecological havenBuilt by the Defoe Shipbuilding Company in Michigan, United States, HMAS Hobart entered service with the Royal Australian Navy in December 1965. During more than 35 years of service, the warship completed three combat deployments during the Vietnam War before being officially decommissioned in May 2000. After its retirement, the Australian Department of Defence gave the vessel to the state of South Australia. The Fleurieu Artificial Reef Society and state authorities prepared the ship for sinking by removing dangerous materials, cutting access points for divers and clearing fuel remains to make sure it was environmentally safe. When explosives were detonated off the Fleurieu Peninsula, the vessel sank upright onto a flat, sandy seabed with few natural rocky features. Its large steel structure, including gun turrets, decks and accessible engine rooms, created vertical surfaces that changed the otherwise flat sea floor. These structures also intercepted nutrient-rich coastal currents, attracting organisms such as sponges, barnacles and soft corals.Scientific findings on reef colonisation and species diversityThe Marine Science team at South Australia’s Department for Environment and Water carried out the biodiversity survey using standard Reef Life Survey underwater visual census methods. Researchers recorded species including snapper, southern blue devil fish, bullseyes and leatherjackets living in and around the wreck. The ship’s steel plates provide shelter from predators and strong tidal flows, creating small habitats at different depths. The reef also benefits from legal protection under the state’s marine park system. The wreck is located inside the Rapid Head Sanctuary Zone within Encounter Marine Park, where both commercial and recreational fishing are banned. According to Department for Environment and Water management guides, rangers patrol the sanctuary to enforce the no-take rules. This allows fish populations and organisms growing on the wreck to develop without pressure from fishing and other forms of human extraction.Eco-tourism and the global artificial reef networkAlongside its conservation role, the ex-HMAS Hobart has become a major destination for experienced divers interested in temperate-water wrecks. The site is unusual among Australia’s artificial naval reefs because divers have regulated access to parts of the ship’s interior, including the original engine room and missile areas. Australia has also sunk several other naval vessels for similar conservation and tourism purposes, including the ex-HMAS Adelaide off New South Wales and the ex-HMAS Canberra off Victoria. International marine studies published in journals including Ecological Engineering and Frontiers in Marine Science have found that well-managed steel shipwrecks can support fish numbers and species diversity similar to nearby natural rocky reefs. By turning retired warships into permanent artificial reefs, environmental agencies can create long-term marine habitats while helping replace natural environments lost along developed coastal areas.

articles.title: In Oklahoma, a veteran spent 5 years fighting back invasive cedars on his 400-acre ranch; now native grasses are returning and water is flowing into newly reappearing streams
articles.summary: Science News: Retired Marine Corps veteran Brian Heishman has been slowly turning a 400-acre ranch near Pawnee, Oklahoma, into a cedar forest for five years. An ove.
articles.body: Retired Marine Corps veteran Brian Heishman has been slowly turning a 400-acre ranch near Pawnee, Oklahoma, into a cedar forest for five years. An overgrown property, choked by Eastern Red Cedars, is showing signs of ecological recovery, with native grasses returning, ponds filling up faster and streams reappearing. For Heishman and his wife, Melinda, the work has become more than just a land management project. After more than two decades of military and government service, it has given Heishman a new calling. According to a USDA report, Heishman served five years in the infantry, 16 years in Explosive Ordnance Disposal and a decade as a U.S. government contractor in Iraq. After retiring from his career of service, he searched for a meaningful way to remain active and then the chance to manage the family property was the opportunity. When Heishman and Melinda bought the land, it had three ponds and large areas thickly covered with Eastern Red Cedars. At first he wondered if he could manage the vast clearing alone, as he had never done such work before. That changed when he cleared a preliminary 500 feet to set up a firebreak for a prescribed burn. This experience gave him the confidence to take on a much larger restoration effort.Working with conservation expertsHeishman started working with Duel Brown, the Pawnee County conservationist for the Natural Resources Conservation Service, who helped find practical ways to improve the property. With the assistance of Cole Fagen of the American Bird Conservancy, Heishman inked his first contract with the NRCS in 2022. Cedar removal has been a fundamental component of his conservation plan ever since. Additional contracts with the NRCS Environmental Quality Incentives Program helped the couple install cross-fencing and grazing practices to better manage their livestock and vegetation. Also, a Farm Service Agency loan for equipment purchases also sped up the cedar-clearing effort. Water management became a priority too. With the help of conservation partners, Heishman restored the dam on the property’s largest pond, improving water availability for cattle. The Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation also helped stock the ponds with fish to enhance their ecological value. And further guidance on the use of prescribed fire was provided by the Pawnee County Prescribed Burn Association.Wildfire accelerates the transitionHeishman’s efforts were accelerated unexpectedly by a wildfire in 2025. The fire also damaged other trees, including oaks and black walnuts, but it destroyed much of the cedar growth on the east side of the property. Heishman is now removing the last of the tree skeletons and allowing the recovering landscape to take hold. Native grasses are starting to come back in areas once filled with cedars. The ponds on the property are filling more quickly and streams that had dried up are starting to flow again, since there is less competition among trees for water. The changes provide a clear measure of how much the land has changed since Heishman’s restoration work began in 2022.Designing a long-term futureRestoration is not a one-time affair for Heishman. His next challenge is to keep the progress and not let the Eastern Red Cedars take back the property. He and Melinda hope to build a home on the ranch one day and enjoy the landscape they have spent years restoring. Their experience also offers a more general lesson for conservation: Landowners don’t have to do big restoration projects all alone. Heishman has transformed an unknown challenge into a long-term stewardship effort by partnering with the NRCS, wildlife agencies, conservation organizations and local prescribed-burn groups. Five years into the project, the changes are becoming more and more apparent. Native grasses are coming back, water is flowing again and a ranch once choked with cedar is slowly being transformed into better range for cattle and wildlife. Restoring the land has become a new way to serve for a veteran who spent much of his life serving others.

articles.title: Gold miners have breached a refuge built for rescued orangutans; 14 hectares of Indonesia’s sanctuary damaged in 3 years
articles.summary: Science News: Illegal gold miners have encroached on Indonesia's Jantho forest reservation, a vital reintroduction site for the critically endangered Sumatran orang.
articles.body: Illegal gold miners have encroached on Indonesia's Jantho forest reservation, a vital reintroduction site for the critically endangered Sumatran orangutan. The country's largest environmental pressure group, Indonesian Forum for the Environment, revealed that miners have breached the forest in Aceh province, where the animals rescued from illegal wildlife trade reside, according to a report by Mongabay. “The result of our monitoring indicates that maybe dozens of excavators are suspected of operating in the Jantho forest area,” said Afifuddin, campaign and advocacy lead at the provincial chapter of the Indonesian Forum for the Environment (Walhi).The Indonesian government established the Jantho orangutan reintroduction area more than 15 years ago within the wider protected forest known as Jantho Nature Reserve. It was in 2011 that conservationists began releasing animals in the area where there were no Sumatran orangutans before. Since then, the Sumatran Orangutan Conservation Programme (SOCP), which works with the Indonesian government on the reintroduction effort, has released nearly 200 orangutans into the forest. It remains one of the country’s most successful release sites for the critically endangered great apes.The Jantho sanctuary was chosen for reintroduction due to its habitat of fig trees, a key food source for orangutans and proximity to the Leuser Ecosystem, which is home to most of the Sumatran orangutans that remain in the wild.But a new analysis by Walhi's Aceh chapter found that approximately 14 hectares of the Jantho Nature Reserve had been damaged by illegal gold mining between 2023 and May 2026, a period in which gold prices more than doubled, from around $1,928 an ounce in early 2023 to more than $4,600 in May 2026. The surge in the price of precious metals has accompanied a global rush for gold as investors seek to insulate wealth from inflation and geopolitical instability, including tensions intensified by the U.S. government and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.Biodiversity at riskThe most recent conservation assessment by IUCN, the global wildlife conservation authority, estimated that 13,846 Sumatran orangutans remain in the wild. But it was conducted in 2017.Moreover, orangutans brought into rescue programs often arrive having suffered trauma from capture and prolonged captivity. The goal of the Jantho site is to return healthy animals to protect forests where they can reproduce and establish self-sustaining wild populations.But their abodes are under pressure right now. Hanif, spokesperson for a coalition of local activist groups known as the Jantho Bergerak Alliance, said illegal mining has increasingly damaged the Jantho reserve over the last three years.Community sources said access to the illegal mining sites likely originated from the Tangse area of Aceh’s Pidie district, located to the east of Jantho. “We urge the government to immediately stop the illegal gold mining taking place in the upstream of the Krueng Aceh Basin, as well as in the Jantho Nature Reserve,” Hanif said.Not just the animals, the pollution from the mining in the watershed of the Krueng Aceh River could also lead to lasting contamination of a crucial water resource, potentially threatening a range of development indicators from child stunting to educational attainment through to adulthood.“The impact isn’t only felt at the mining site, but also in the communities who use the river as a source of clean water, irrigation for farming, and fisheries,” Afifuddin said.Darwin, Jantho’s imum mukim, an Acehnese traditional community leader, said the community stance against illegal mining had been decided after a meeting of 13 villages in Jantho. “We have held discussions with village heads, community leaders, youth leaders, and youth representatives. As a result, we agreed to reject all illegal mining activities and illegal mining in the upstream area of the Krueng Aceh,” Darwin said on June 29.Darwin said pollution meant many residents had experienced difficulties catching fish, while households relying on river water faced new problems in obtaining drinking water. In April, the community reported illegal mining to the Aceh Besar district police and the provincial conservation department, the BKSDA. From June 16-20, a joint operation by the police, the BKSDA, the forestry ministry’s law enforcement division (Gakkum), and the local community conducted spot inspections of the suspected mining sites.However, the search found no heavy equipment operating in the nature reserve. Instead, the team put up warning signs and razed a mining encampment in addition to destroying some light equipment found at the scene.An endangered speciesSumatran orangutans typically give birth to a single offspring nine years apart, with the longest interbirth interval of any of the apes. Thus, along with mining, the species' recovery is hampered by an exceptionally slow reproductive rate.“Significant areas of the orangutan’s range are seriously threatened by logging, mining concessions and agricultural plantations, while new roads are continuously being cut through the habitat,” the IUCN noted in its 2017 assessment. “If the rate of decline observed since 1985 and predicted continues unabated, the population decline will exceed 80% over a three-generation period,” the IUCN warned.For orangutans and the conservationists working to support them, the Jantho reintroduction forest is a place of hope: On May 22, fieldworkers confirmed that Bulan, a female orangutan rescued from traffickers and returned to the wild seven years ago, had given birth in the Jantho reservation. This was the 11th live birth recorded by the charity managing the reintroduction in partnership with the Indonesian government.The area is also home to siamang gibbons (Symphalangus syndactylus), sun bears (Helarctos malayanus), and dozens of rare bird species.“Monitoring of conservation areas will continue to be tightened through routine patrols and coordination with law enforcement and local governments to prevent the resumption of illegal mining activities,” said Ujang from the Aceh conservation department.

articles.title: Meet Lilah Mehta, the Connecticut high-school student who entered a Yale lab at 16 and is already a co-author of published research
articles.summary: Science News: When Lilah Mehta entered a biomedical research laboratory at Yale University as a 16-year-old high-school pupil, her main goal was to explore the biol.
articles.body: When Lilah Mehta entered a biomedical research laboratory at Yale University as a 16-year-old high-school pupil, her main goal was to explore the biological questions that had interested her since her ninth-grade science classes. Two years later, the New Canaan resident and King School student in Stamford has reached an academic milestone rarely achieved before university: co-authoring a peer-reviewed neuroscience study with senior researchers at the Yale School of Medicine. Mehta’s academic journey and research work were featured in Moffly Media’s annual Teens to Watch 2026 profile series, published by New Canaan, Darien & Rowayton Magazine. The series recognised her as one of Fairfield County’s standout students. The high-school senior directly contributed to a scientific review paper published in the medical journal Current Opinion in Immunology. The study looks at the Kv1.3 voltage-gated potassium channel, an ion channel found on immune cells that researchers believe may help control neuroinflammation linked to Alzheimer’s disease and other neurodegenerative conditions. Working under Dr Srikant Rangaraju in the Department of Neurology at Yale School of Medicine, Mehta worked with a team of immunologists and neuroscientists. Her work included reviewing complex molecular research and studying network datasets to understand how Kv1.3 channels interact within brain microglial cells and peripheral T cells.Navigating laboratory setbacks and complex molecular scienceMehta’s move into advanced neuroscience came with several technical challenges. During her early experiments, the laboratory faced repeated problems, including cases where cell cultures were lost because of unexpected contamination. Looking back at her laboratory experience, Mehta said dealing with uncertain results changed how she approached scientific research. "My research hit many bumps over the years, particularly in the lab; the cell batches died twice due to fungal infections," Mehta said in an interview published by Moffly Media. "I have found research is rarely a linear path; you have to remain flexible and be comfortable with things not always going as planned, regardless of how carefully you design a study." Despite these early problems, Mehta stayed focused on understanding scientific research. She spent hours using databases such as PubMed and ScienceDirect to learn unfamiliar biomedical concepts. "The same curiosity I had back in 9th-grade biology has sustained me throughout my Independent Study and STEM Scholars project," Mehta recalled. "I approach ScienceDirect and PubMed articles expecting to encounter gaps in my knowledge and to correct some of my previous assumptions. I often bump into terms I've never heard before—what even is ferroptosis, anyway? —and happily dive down rabbit holes to discover not just answers, but many more questions." Her continued work eventually became part of the Yale team’s published paper, titled Functional interactions of Kv1.3 channels in microglia and T cells and their implications in neurodegeneration. The paper explores possible treatments that target Kv1.3 channels to influence both innate and adaptive immune responses in people with neurodegenerative diseases.Recognition at state level and academic foundationsMehta’s research skills have also earned recognition at regional and state science competitions in Connecticut. She was named a finalist in the Life Sciences category at the Connecticut Science and Engineering Fair and presented her findings at the Health and Science Symposium at the University of Connecticut Health Center. At King School in Stamford, Mehta takes part in the school’s Advanced Science Program with Independent Research and Engineering (ASPIRE), led by Dr Victoria Schulman. The programme connects motivated high-school pupils with academic mentors at regional research universities, giving students the chance to carry out real laboratory experiments alongside doctoral candidates and postdoctoral researchers. School officials said student-led projects such as Mehta’s are helping raise the standard of high-school science education across the state. Alongside her biomedical research, Mehta is involved in school community projects, including SPARC, a research group focused on studying and improving student life on campus. She also leads local community service projects with her sisters, balancing her demanding scientific work with volunteering. Asked about her long-term goals, Mehta said her laboratory experience has strengthened her interest in pursuing medicine and environmental science. "That really solidified my interest in medicine, exciting me with the prospect of working with like-minded professionals on intensely meaningful problems," Mehta told Moffly Media, adding that she hopes to use her scientific background to create positive and practical change in public health and environmental sustainability.

articles.title: In 1989, Detroit Zoo began helping save snails wiped out in the wild; 37 years later, 500 are travelling 5,000 miles to Tahiti, part of a program that has returned 17,000
articles.summary: Science News: A conservation effort that began nearly four decades ago is sending hundreds of tiny snails on a remarkable journey back to their native home. Five hu.
articles.body: A conservation effort that began nearly four decades ago is sending hundreds of tiny snails on a remarkable journey back to their native home. Five hundred Partula snails raised at the Detroit Zoo are travelling more than 5,000 miles from Michigan to Tahiti, where they will be released into the wild as part of a long-running effort to restore populations of these endangered native snails. According to the Detroit Zoological Society, the latest shipment is part of an international conservation program that has returned more than 17,000 Partula snails to their native islands. The Detroit Zoo has been involved in the effort since 1989, helping breed and care for the snails after invasive predators caused their populations to collapse in the wild. The broader program has helped return 11 Partula species that were once considered extinct in the wild.A decades-long effortPartula snails are small, tree-dwelling mollusks native to islands in French Polynesia. Although they may seem insignificant compared with larger endangered animals, several Partula species faced a severe population collapse after an invasive predator was introduced to the islands. The predator was the rosy wolf snail, which had itself been brought to the islands in an attempt to control another invasive snail. Instead, it preyed on native Partula snails, contributing to the disappearance of several species from the wild.The crisis prompted conservationists and zoos to establish captive populations. The Detroit Zoo became involved in this work in 1989, helping breed and care for Partula snails with the eventual goal of returning them to their natural environment. That work has continued for 37 years.500 snails head homeFive hundred adult Partula snails raised at the Detroit Zoo are beginning their journey from Royal Oak, Michigan, to Tahiti. The trip covers more than 5,000 miles, but the journey is more than simply moving captive animals from one location to another. The snails are being sent as part of a coordinated effort to rebuild populations in the forests where their species originally lived. Before leaving, each snail receives a small orange dot of animal-safe paint on its shell. The marking is designed to glow under ultraviolet light, allowing conservationists in Tahiti to distinguish the 2026 release group from snails released in previous years. A different paint colour is used for each year's release, giving researchers a practical way to track individual release groups after they enter the wild.From captivity to forestsFor Partula nodosa, the stakes are particularly significant. The species is currently classified as Extinct in the Wild, meaning it survives under human care but does not have a known surviving wild population. Conservation breeding provides a way to prevent such species from disappearing completely. Zoos and other institutions can maintain genetically viable populations while conservationists work to create conditions for their eventual return.According to the Detroit Zoo, its conservation partners have documented wild-born offspring following earlier Partula reintroductions. Such reproduction is an important step because simply releasing captive-bred animals is not enough to establish a self-sustaining population. The animals must survive, reproduce and contribute to future generations in their native habitat.More than 17,000 returnedThe 500 snails travelling to Tahiti represent only a small part of the broader recovery program. According to the Detroit Zoological Society, more than 17,000 Partula snails have been reintroduced through the collaborative effort. The program has also returned 11 Partula species that were once considered extinct in the wild to their native islands. That figure illustrates how conservation programs can operate over long periods. Instead of producing an immediate result, captive breeding and reintroduction can require years of animal care, monitoring and repeated releases. For the Detroit Zoo, the current shipment is another stage in a program that connects its animal-care facilities in Michigan with conservation sites thousands of miles away in French Polynesia.Protecting more than a speciesThe importance of Partula recovery also extends beyond biodiversity. The Detroit Zoological Society notes that Partula snails have cultural significance in Polynesia. Their distinctive shells have been associated with different islands, giving the animals a place in the region's cultural heritage. Their return therefore represents more than restoring populations of small forest snails. It also helps reconnect native wildlife with the ecosystems and cultural landscapes where these species evolved. After 37 years of captive breeding and conservation work, the latest 500 snails are now taking another step toward that goal. Their journey from Michigan to Tahiti shows how a species that disappeared from the wild can, with sustained international cooperation, begin making its way back.

articles.title: 2025's Megaquake Appears to Have Awakened a Volcano That Was Dormant For 500 Years
articles.summary: The gift that keeps on giving.
articles.body:
For nearly five centuries, the Krasheninnikov volcano in Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula had not erupted. Nor did it seem particularly interested in doing so.

Then, just before midday on 30 July 2025 local time, off Kamchatka's coast, Earth's crust abruptly tripped over itself.

The megathrust quake was one of the most powerful ever recorded, registering a magnitude of 8.8. Tsunami warnings were issued around the world, and across the peninsula, several volcanoes roared to life , spewing ash and lava in what officials called an " eruption parade ".

Kamchatka is one of the most volcanic places on Earth, home to some 160 volcanoes, 29 of which are classified as active , so geophysical pyrotechnics are not outside the norm.

But one of the volcanoes joining the pandemonium was, in fact, a surprise. Krasheninnikov had not erupted for centuries ; yet, several days after the megaquake, it started belching out an enormous plume .

It's not unreasonable to assume that the two events were connected; but now, a team led by volcanologist James Hickey of the University of Exeter in the UK has studied the eruption and worked out how the Kamchatka megaquake may have rattled Krasheninnikov out of its slumber.

"The prolonged earthquake shaking likely promoted time-dependent volatile exsolution, bubble growth, and eventual reservoir destabilization in a system already mechanically susceptible to failure," they write in a preprint uploaded to EarthArXiv ahead of peer review .

"We show that apparently quiescent volcanoes may conceal hidden critical states prone to seismic perturbation, particularly in extensional arc settings with volatile-rich magmas exposed to repeated megathrust earthquakes."

Earthquakes and volcanic outbursts can go hand-in-hand… but getting from one to the other isn't quite so straightforward, and Kamchatka is the perfect demonstration.

The region sits above a subduction zone, where the Pacific Plate plunges beneath the Okhotsk microplate, generating both its extraordinary volcanism and its powerful earthquakes.

If the equation were as simple as "insert earthquake, get volcano", the results of the Kamchatka megaquake should have been dramatically more explosive. Dozens of potentially active volcanoes felt the shaking – yet only a handful participated in the eruption parade.

Some of the volcanoes involved should hardly raise an eyebrow; for example, Karymsky has been erupting almost continuously since 1996 ; it would be stranger if it suddenly piped down.

But why Krasheninnikov? And why, after 475 years of silence, now?

By all outward appearances, there was nothing particularly unusual about Krasheninnikov before the earthquake.

Nine years of satellite radar observations showed no swelling of the ground that would suggest magma was accumulating beneath the volcano. In fact, the surface was slowly sinking, at a rate of around 4 millimeters a year.

Nor could satellites detect any sulfur dioxide escaping from Krasheninnikov before the earthquake, even as they picked up the gas pouring from other volcanoes across Kamchatka.

Roughly two days later, 12 earthquakes of around magnitude 4 rattled the area around Krasheninnikov in the space of just five hours. Satellite observations revealed what was happening underground: Magma was forcing open a near-vertical fracture in the crust.

The resulting dyke intrusion involved an estimated 32 million cubic meters (1.13 billion cubic feet) of magma, fed from a reservoir around 6 kilometers (3.7 miles) beneath the surface.

You'd think that all this ballyhoo would simply shake the volcano hard enough to burst it open – but the permanent stress changes at Krasheninnikov were minuscule – just 0.01 to 0.05 megapascals in Coulomb stress. Magma reservoirs are generally thought to require overpressures around 1 to 10 megapascals to fail.

The transient stress while the quake was physically shaking the ground was larger – around 1.0 ± 0.6 megapascals, potentially just large enough in theory to wake the slumbering volcano. But the researchers don't think that's what actually happened.

For one thing, Krasheninnikov didn't respond immediately. The magma didn't start forcing its way into the dyke until an estimated 1.5 to 2.5 days after the earthquake.

According to their modeling, the magma in the reservoir had properties consistent with high gas content. And that may be where those 475 years of silence become important.

Over centuries of crystallization, volatile-rich magma may have accumulated bubbles in the reservoir. The prolonged shaking of the earthquake could then have encouraged more gas to diffuse into those bubbles, making them grow, while also helping new bubbles form.

Like your tummy after too much carbonated beverage, all that expanding gas increases the pressure. Eventually, the researchers propose, the reservoir became unstable, magma forced its way into the dyke, and Krasheninnikov erupted.

Earth burped, and a long-dormant volcano was startled awake.

This could help explain why Krasheninnikov, of all Kamchatka's volcanoes, responded to the earthquake.

Although it appeared quiet at the surface, its volatile-rich magma and the extensional tectonic environment beneath the volcano may have left its reservoir unusually susceptible to disturbance.

The researchers call this a "hidden critical state" – the volcano may have been primed for eruption in ways that weren't visible in the usual warning signs of seismic activity, ground deformation, or escaping gas.

And that could have implications beyond Kamchatka. A volcano that appears peacefully dormant may not necessarily be as stable underground as it looks – and the right earthquake trigger could provide the disturbance that tips an already vulnerable system over the edge.

"Ultimately, the earthquake likely facilitated the eruption not by directly forcing immediate reservoir failure, but by imposing prolonged dynamic stresses on a volatile-rich and mechanically susceptible magmatic system, prompting delayed volatile exsolution, bubble growth, reservoir destabilization, and later dyke intrusion and eruption," the researchers write .

The findings can be read on EarthArXiv .

articles.title: A pigeon with a ‘bleeding heart’ has returned after 20 years: Rare Philippine bird spotted in 2026, but why its comeback may not be good news
articles.summary: Science News: A camera on the Philippine island of Mindoro captured one of the country's rarest birds, confirming that the critically endangered Mindoro bleeding-he.
articles.body: A camera on the Philippine island of Mindoro captured one of the country's rarest birds, confirming that the critically endangered Mindoro bleeding-heart pigeon still survives in the wild. The bird was spotted in August in the Puerto Galera rainforest, and is the first confirmed photograph of the species Gallicolumba platenae in two decades, according to the nonprofit organisation Centre for Conservation Innovation Ph Inc. (CCIPH). “For an extremely rare and secretive species, a single image can carry enormous weight,” CCIPH researchers wrote in a September 3 announcement. “It confirms that the bird continues to survive within the landscape.”The photograph resulted from an Indigenous-led initiative inside the Iraya Mangyan ancestral domain. CCIPH attributed it to Iraya patrollers Alex, Melenciano, Cristito, Jay, and Sonnyboy, citing their landscape knowledge, sustained forest presence, and stewardship of their ancestral domain. Working with them, CCIPH researchers John Bibar and Joshua Manila deployed the camera traps under the Mindoro Forest and Biodiversity Conservation Programme.“This record not only proves that this very rare species continues to persist in these steep rainforests, but solidifies the importance of Puerto Galera as a UNESCO biosphere reserve and an important sanctuary for this critically endangered species,” said Juan Carlos Gonzalez, an ornithologist and curator for birds at the Museum of Natural History at the University of the Philippines Los Baños, to Mongabay.The orange-red spot on the bird's otherwise white chest along with the iridescent green plumage on its head and neck, makes it readily identifiable. Gonzalez also pointed to its blue-green and brown upper parts, brown wings and single whitish wing bar, which distinguish it from other Philippine bleeding hearts. They are also called 'bleeding heart' because they have a vivid red or orange patch of feathers on their white chest that looks like an open, bleeding wound.Decades of absenceThe Mindoro bleeding-heart is a ground-dwelling pigeon endemic to Mindoro. While historical accounts described it as common in the island's forests, confirmed encounters became extremely rare during the second half of the 20th century. The last confirmed record came in 2005, when an individual was caught in a snare intended for red junglefowl near a fruiting fig tree. Other encounters were subsequently reported, but not all could be verified, CCIPH said.The prolonged absence led the Search for Lost Birds program to list the pigeon as a “lost” species, a designation covering birds not documented by science for at least 10 years. The bird is also listed as critically endangered on the IUCN Red List, meaning it faces an extremely high risk of extinction. “Birds that find themselves on both these lists are of particular concern,” said Alex Berryman, who oversees species conservation assessments for Asia at the NGO BirdLife International.New records setThe species has generally been described as a lowland forest specialist, typically occurring at elevations of around 400 meters (1,300 feet), and occasionally up to 800 m (2,600 ft). But the camera trap photographed it above 900 m (nearly 3,000 ft). “A lowland specialist appearing in high-elevation forest is not necessarily a species expanding its horizons,” CCIPH researchers wrote. “It may be a species running out of lowland to live in.”Moist lowland and transitional mid-mountain rainforest can still occur at around 900 m in the steep range, Gonzalez said. Much of the lower slopes of Puerto Galera have been degraded as tourism grows, potentially pushing the birds toward less-accessible upper forests. Berryman said the high-elevation record “raises hope that there might be more out there.”Protecting the speciesHowever, the spotting is not all positive as the birds' habitat, the forest, is under threat as well. Berryman said the next priorities should be to safeguard as much suitable habitat as possible and conduct a comprehensive assessment of the species' population. Gonzalez called for establishing a legislated protected area covering the Mount Halcon-Mount Malasimbo Range, which he said currently has no government-designated protected area covering its entirety.Moreover, he also called for a stop to illegal logging and poaching, strengthening conservation education and preventing traps intended for red junglefowl from catching bleeding-hearts. He proposed safer trap designs and using Indigenous wildlife-tracking expertise to support regulated ecotourism.“Whether it continues to beat for another twenty years or another hundred will depend on whether we treat this image merely as an extraordinary record or allow the evidence it carries to change what we do next,” the CCIPH researchers wrote.

articles.title: Cientistas criam as primeiras cachorros hipoalergênicos do mundo | G1
articles.standfirst: Duas beagles nasceram nos EUA sem a proteína responsável pela maioria das alergias a cães, eliminada por técnica de CRISPR.
articles.summary: Duas beagles nasceram nos EUA sem a proteína responsável pela maioria das alergias a cães, eliminada por técnica de CRISPR.
articles.body:
Cães com edição genética são os primeiros hipoalergênicos — Foto: Divulgação

Quem tem alergia a cachorro, mas sonha em ter um cão de estimação, ganhou um motivo real para ter esperança. Uma equipe de cientistas conseguiu, pela primeira vez, editar geneticamente cães para eliminar a proteína responsável pela maioria das reações alérgicas em humanos, e o resultado já anda por aí em quatro patas: duas beagles saudáveis que provam que a técnica funciona.

A pesquisa foi feita pela empresa americana Kindred Companion Sciences, que se tornou a primeira a eliminar um alérgeno em cães vivos, não apenas em células de laboratório.

Os animais estão bem e vivendo com saúde com tutores nos Estados Unidos. A pesquisa abre uma esperança para quem tem esse tipo de alergia, mas os especialistas dizem que ainda são necessários outros estudos.

Dono com alergia a cachorro pode ter animal após edição genética — Foto: Divulgação

O que os pesquisadores estão tentando fazer é resolver esse problema com edição genética, eliminando a proteína fabricada nas glândulas da saliva e na língua dos cães. Ela também aparece no pelo e na caspa, porque os cães se lambem constantemente e espalham saliva pelo próprio corpo.

Com isso, mesmo que cães que soltam menos pelo sejam frequentemente considerados hipoalergênicos, eles ainda têm essas proteínas que, espalhadas pelo corpo, causam a reação alérgica.

Em pessoas alérgicas, o sistema imunológico identifica essa proteína como uma ameaça e produz anticorpos (as chamadas IgE) para combatê-la. É essa reação exagerada que causa coceira, olhos vermelhos, espirros e crises de chiado no peito.

A Can f 1 é considerada o principal alérgeno canino: está presente na maioria dos casos de sensibilização a cachorros, segundo estudos anteriores. Por isso, ela virou o alvo natural para quem tentasse resolver o problema pela raiz — e não apenas tratar os sintomas de quem já é alérgico.

Cães estão saudáveis e vem sendo acompanhados — Foto: Divulgação

O processo não envolveu cruzamento seletivo nem alteração genética em cães adultos. Os pesquisadores usaram células de um feto de beagle e editaram, dentro delas, o gene responsável pela Can f 1.

A ferramenta usada para isso foi o CRISPR, uma tecnologia que funciona como uma espécie de tesoura molecular guiada por GPS.

Ela localiza um trecho exato do DNA — no caso, o gene que fabrica a Can f 1 — e faz um corte preciso naquele ponto. O sistema é formado por duas partes:

Uma molécula de RNA que serve de guia até o endereço certo no genoma

Uma enzima, a Cas9, que executa o corte.

No caso das beagles, o corte feito pelo CRISPR provocou uma pequena inserção de DNA que bagunça a leitura do restante do gene — uma mutação chamada frameshift — e impede a célula de fabricar a proteína.

Só depois dessa edição as células do feto foram usadas para clonar os animais, por meio de uma técnica chamada transferência nuclear de célula somática, a mesma família de método que gerou a ovelha Dolly, em 1996.

As duas filhotes, batizadas Alfie e Bailey, nasceram em setembro de 2024 com peso normal para a raça e não apresentaram problemas de desenvolvimento nos exames veterinários realizados até a publicação do estudo.

Para confirmar que a ausência da proteína realmente evitava a reação alérgica, os cientistas fizeram um teste cutâneo em um voluntário humano com alergia a cães já diagnosticada. O extrato do animal editado não provocou reação nenhuma.

Bailey mora com o tutor em Nova York e Alfie mora na Florida com o tutor. Os dois seguem sendo acompanhados.

A pesquisa é promissora e a empresa está pleiteando a patente da tecnologia. No entanto, ainda não é tão simples que isso seja trazido do laboratório para a vida real ainda são necessárias outras pesquisas, com testes de reação em número maior de voluntários, por exemplo.

articles.title: A huge forested island appeared in a British Columbia reservoir, vanished, then resurfaced 30 km away 15 days later with trees, birds and other animals still aboard
articles.summary: Science News: In the summer of 2026, workers and residents around the Williston Reservoir in northern British Columbia witnessed something that sounded like folklor.
articles.body: In the summer of 2026, workers and residents around the Williston Reservoir in northern British Columbia witnessed something that sounded like folklore: a large, forested island broke free from the shoreline, drifted across the lake, disappeared from view, and then turned up again about 30 kilometres away, still carrying mature trees, nesting birds and other wildlife. The “ghost island,” as some locals began calling it, had broken loose from saturated, peaty soils along the reservoir’s edge and been carried by wind and currents before grounding again downstream. As reported by Smithsonian Magazine, the event has captivated the public and prompted scientists to study how climate change, reservoir operations and fragile northern soils may be creating more of these drifting landmasses.A reservoir in a remote, changing landscapeThe Williston Reservoir, formed by the W.A.C. Bennett Dam on the Peace River, is one of the largest man-made lakes in North America. It stretches more than 170 kilometres through a rugged, boreal landscape of spruce, pine, wetlands and peatlands. The region is remote, sparsely populated and rich in wildlife, including bears, moose, waterfowl and numerous songbirds.Like many northern ecosystems, this area is warming faster than the global average. Permafrost is thawing, precipitation patterns are shifting and reservoir levels fluctuate in response to hydropower demands and seasonal inflows. All of these factors affect shoreline stability, soil saturation and the way vegetation anchors, or fails to anchor, to the ground.The island’s first appearanceThe story began when reservoir operators and local observers noticed a new island where none had existed before. It was not a small sandbar or gravel spit, but a substantial chunk of land: dozens of metres across, covered with mature trees, shrubs and soil, and already being used by birds and other animals.At first, many assumed it was a previously submerged feature exposed by dropping water levels. But as days passed, the “island” did not stay put. Instead, it began to move, slowly drifting away from the shore as if it were a giant raft. That’s when it became clear: this was not a fixed island at all, but a massive slab of soil and vegetation that had detached from the shoreline and was floating on the reservoir.How a forest can floatFloating islands are rare but not unknown. They form when thick mats of vegetation, roots, peat and soil become buoyant enough to lift off the underlying substrate and ride on the water’s surface. In northern peatlands, this process is facilitated by: thick layers of partially decayed plant material (peat) that are light and spongy; high water tables that saturate soils and reduce friction between layers; and root systems that bind the surface mat together, allowing it to move as a single unit.Around reservoirs, additional factors come into play. Fluctuating water levels can undercut shorelines, while wind and wave action can pry loose large sections of vegetated soil. When conditions align, an entire forested patch can break free and begin to drift.The 15-day journey across WillistonOnce detached, the island was carried by a combination of wind, currents and possibly seiches (standing waves) in the reservoir. Over about 15 days, it travelled roughly 30 kilometres from its point of origin, moving slowly but steadily across open water.During this time, the island was not just a passive object. It remained intact enough to support mature trees, including spruce and other conifers, still rooted in the soil mat; shrubs and ground vegetation that continued to grow and transpire; birds that nested or roosted on the island, treating it like any other piece of land; and small mammals, insects and possibly amphibians that rode along within the soil and vegetation.For observers on the water and along the shore, the sight was surreal: a moving patch of forest, complete with wildlife, gliding across a vast reservoir.Disappearance and rediscoveryAt one point during its journey, the island slipped out of sight—either drifting behind a point of land, into a less-monitored arm of the reservoir, or simply becoming hard to distinguish from the surrounding shoreline vegetation. For a time, it seemed to have vanished, fuelling local speculation and storytelling.Then, about 15 days after it was first spotted, the island was observed again, now grounded along a different section of the reservoir roughly 30 kilometres from where it started. It had not broken apart or sunk; the trees were still standing, the soil mat was still coherent, and animals were still using it. In effect, a functioning ecosystem had hitched a ride across the lake and set down in a new location.Why scientists are paying attentionEvents like this are more than curiosities; they are indicators of how northern landscapes are responding to changing conditions. Researchers are interested in several questions, like:How often are floating islands forming in the Williston and other northern reservoirs?What role do thawing permafrost, saturated peat and reservoir level fluctuations play in detaching these landmasses?How far can they travel, and where do they ultimately end up?What are the implications for wildlife, carbon storage and reservoir operations?Floating islands can transport nutrients, seeds and organisms to new areas, potentially altering local ecosystems. They can also pose navigational hazards for boats and, if they break up, release pulses of organic material into the water. In a warming north, such phenomena may become more common.A symbol of a landscape in motionFor local residents and workers, the drifting island is both fascinating and unsettling. It underscores how dynamic the reservoir shoreline can be, and how climate change is making familiar landscapes feel less stable. Trees that once seemed firmly rooted can, under the right (or wrong) conditions, become passengers on a slow, watery journey.At the same time, the island’s survival—carrying trees, birds and other animals across 30 kilometres of open water—speaks to the resilience of these ecosystems. Even when detached from the ground, the living community held together, adapted and found a new place to rest.What comes nextIn the wake of the island’s reappearance, scientists and reservoir managers are discussing how to monitor similar events in the future. Possibilities include: using satellite imagery and drone surveys to detect new floating islands early; tracking their movement with GPS tags or markers where feasible; studying the soil and vegetation composition to understand what makes some patches more likely to detach; and incorporating floating-island dynamics into reservoir management and climate adaptation plans.For now, the Williston’s “ghost island” remains a striking example of how quickly and dramatically northern landscapes can change. In a single summer, a forested island appeared, vanished and reappeared dozens of kilometres away, carrying its trees and tenants with it: a reminder that in a warming world, even the ground beneath our feet may not stay where we expect it to.A huge forested island appeared in a British Columbia reservoir, vanished, then resurfaced 30 km away 15 days later with trees, birds and other animals still aboard

articles.title: A ‘devil flower’ with no leaves, no branches, no green part has been discovered in a Thai forest, scientists say its bizarre appearance is hiding an even stranger secret
articles.summary: Science News: It has no leaves, no branches and no green parts, and spends much of its life concealed beneath fallen leaves on the forest floor. Scientists have now.
articles.body: It has no leaves, no branches and no green parts, and spends much of its life concealed beneath fallen leaves on the forest floor. Scientists have now described a bizarre new flowering plant from Thailand, naming it Thismia daemona, the “devil flower”, for its dark, horn-like appearance. Details of the discovery were reported by Pensoft Publishers, while the research paper, Thismia daemona (Thismiaceae), a new species from Thailand supported by morphological and molecular evidence, was published in PhytoKeys and is also indexed on DeepDyve. Found in Thong Pha Phum National Park in western Thailand, the plant belongs to Thismia, a genus of tiny, unusual flowering plants sometimes known as “fairy lanterns”. Unlike ordinary green plants, Thismia daemona contains no chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise. Instead, it obtains nutrients through underground fungi, remaining hidden beneath leaf litter for most of its life.A flower that doesn’t behave like an ordinary plantThe most remarkable thing about the new species is what it lacks. Because Thismia daemona is achlorophyllous, it contains no chlorophyll and therefore cannot photosynthesise. Instead, it relies on underground fungal partners for nutrients, a lifestyle known as mycoheterotrophy.Its roots are described as coral-like, while the plant’s above-ground portion consists largely of its unusual flower emerging from the leaf litter. The species was found growing beneath the shade of lower montane forest, alongside small bamboo, at an elevation of about 950–970 metres.That habitat is significant. Species of Thismia are more commonly associated with humid, lowland rainforest environments. The discovery of T. daemona in a seasonal, mountainous forest at nearly 1,000 metres therefore came as a surprise to the researchers.Why does it look so strange?The flower’s appearance explains its dramatic scientific name. It is predominantly blackish, with reddish-orange, fleshy structures around the outside. At the top is a dome-like structure known as a mitre, crowned by three slender appendages.The combination gives the flower an almost fantastical appearance, more like something from a dark forest tale than a conventional flowering plant. The researchers examined fresh and preserved specimens under a microscope and also conducted molecular analyses using nuclear and mitochondrial genetic markers to establish that the plant represents a distinct species. Their findings place it within Thismia section Geomitra, where it is closely related to Thismia betung-kerihunensis.The discovery expands the range of a rare plant groupThe find is important beyond the identification of one new species. Before Thismia daemona was described, section Geomitra was known from Peninsular Malaysia, Borneo and Sumatra. Its presence in Thailand extends the known northern range of the entire group. The new species also brings the number of Thismia species recorded in Thailand to 16, according to the research report.Fewer than 50 plants are knownThe discovery comes with a warning, however. Researchers currently know of just one population, comprising fewer than 50 individuals and occupying an area smaller than a football field. Because of its extremely restricted known distribution and the vulnerability of its habitat, the scientists have assessed Thismia daemona as Critically Endangered under IUCN Red List criteria.Although the plants occur inside a national park, protection on paper does not necessarily eliminate the risks facing such a specialised species. Its tiny population and dependence on particular forest and fungal conditions make it especially vulnerable to changes in its microhabitat. The researchers say conservation will therefore need to involve the surrounding communities as well as formal protection.For now, the discovery of Thismia daemona offers a glimpse into one of the forest’s least visible worlds, a plant that abandoned leaves and sunlight, lives largely out of sight and depends on fungi underground, yet produces one of the most striking flowers botanists have encountered in Thailand.

articles.title: Scientists used fossil wings, lasers and AI to recreate the calls of insects from 165 million years ago; some Jurassic species were already communicating above human hearing
articles.summary: Science News: For 165 million years, the sounds made by insects living alongside dinosaurs were lost to time. Scientists have now recreated some of those calls usin.
articles.body: For 165 million years, the sounds made by insects living alongside dinosaurs were lost to time. Scientists have now recreated some of those calls using fossilised wings, studies of living insects, computer modelling and artificial intelligence.According to Smithsonian Magazine, the research focused on nine extinct insect species related to modern crickets and katydids. The team studied 20 fossil specimens found in Inner Mongolia, China. The fossils preserved important details of the insects’ wings, including structures that were used to produce sound.Researchers say the results offer the best evidence-based approximation so far of what part of a Jurassic forest may have sounded like. Their work was published on August 25 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, along with audio samples of the reconstructed calls.The work also revealed something unexpected. One of the insects, Sigmaboilus peregrinus, appears to have produced sounds between 20 and 22 kilohertz. That is at or above the upper limit of human hearing and means some Jurassic insects may already have been using ultrasonic communication.How Jurassic insects communicatedUnlike humans, crickets, grasshoppers and katydids do not use vocal cords to produce their familiar calls. They use a process called stridulation, which involves rubbing body parts with ridged surfaces against each other.In modern grasshoppers and katydids, a leg can be dragged across a wing. Crickets usually move one wing across the other. The Jurassic insects studied by the researchers had similar structures on their wings.One wing had comb-like ridges, while the other had a scraping structure. When the two surfaces moved against each other, the scraper caught the ridges and produced a series of rapid clicks. These clicks blended together into a continuous chirp.The exact structure of the wings affected the sound. The number and spacing of the ridges, along with the size of the area that vibrated, helped determine the pitch and rhythm of each call.That made the fossilised wings especially useful to scientists. “The beauty of fossil insects is that they can preserve their instruments and receptors on their tough external skeleton, unlike many other animals,” Edmund Jarzembowski, an associate scientist at London’s Natural History Museum who was not involved in the study, told Smithsonian magazine.Lasers helped reconstruct callsThe scientists first studied how living insects produce sound. They used high-speed cameras and a technique called laser Doppler vibrometry to measure how modern insects’ wings moved and vibrated during stridulation.Those measurements were then used to build and test a computer model. The model showed how differences in wing structures could affect the sounds produced by the insects.The researchers then created two-dimensional models of the fossilised wings and fed their structural information into the computer model. They also considered the evolutionary relationships between the extinct insects and their living relatives.Machine learning was then used to help predict the patterns of the ancient calls. The process produced nine different reconstructed sounds linked to the nine fossil species.Most of the insects appear to have produced relatively low-frequency calls, similar to those made by modern crickets. Their calls were around five kilohertz. Many were described as “pure tone” sounds, meaning they were mainly made up of one frequency.The result would have been clear, high-pitched chirps rather than the hissing or buzzing sounds people may associate with some insects.Calls above human hearingThe most striking finding came from Sigmaboilus peregrinus. The researchers' reconstruction suggested that it could produce a call between 20 and 22 kilohertz.Humans generally hear sounds from about 20 hertz to 20 kilohertz. Sounds above that range are known as ultrasonic sounds.“The first time we reconstructed the song and saw it was over 20 kilohertz, we were so excited,” Jun-Jie Gu, a professor of entomology at Sichuan Agricultural University, said, as quoted by New York Times.The finding challenges a long-standing explanation for why some insects evolved ultrasonic communication. Scientists have suggested that bats may have driven the development of these high-frequency calls because insects could use them to communicate while avoiding predators.But bats appeared on Earth roughly 100 million years after the end of the Jurassic. That means they could not have been responsible for the development of ultrasonic calls in these much older insects.Gu and his colleagues instead suggest that Jurassic insects may have had other reasons to use higher frequencies. One possibility was avoiding predators such as early mammals and other animals.Another was competition between insects. If many species were calling at the same frequency, their signals could have become difficult to distinguish.Gu said the insects may have wanted to “have their own channels”. He added that “165 million years ago, the insect community may have already had sophisticated acoustic niches- multiple species occupying different frequency bands from low to high”.Researchers say the work could also help scientists reconstruct sounds made by other extinct insects. Jarzembowski suggested that AI could eventually be used to study ancient beetles and ants as well.“Perhaps AI will help us reconstruct other insect songs, too,” he said. “Let’s look more closely at their fossils, as there’s a potential paleo-orchestra to be discovered.”Gu said the research could also help create more scientifically accurate portrayals of the Jurassic. His team worked with the creators of a new Netflix documentary mini-series, “The Dinosaurs”, to add reconstructed insect sounds to its Jurassic scenes.Thomas Land, a zoologist who worked as a researcher on the series, said the insect sounds helped create a more accurate Jurassic setting. “It’s such a small detail,” he said, “but we did it because every choice like that makes the whole much more realistic.”

articles.title: White storks vanished from Southern Sweden in the 1950s; a wetland revival now aims to support 100 breeding pairs
articles.summary: Science News: White storks once formed a familiar part of the landscape in southern Sweden, but by 1954 the species had disappeared as a breeding bird from the coun.
articles.body: White storks once formed a familiar part of the landscape in southern Sweden, but by 1954 the species had disappeared as a breeding bird from the country. Their decline was closely linked to dramatic changes in the countryside, where wetlands were drained and other habitats altered over generations. In response, ‘Naturskyddsföreningen Skåne’(Swedish Society for Nature Conservation Skåne) and its partners began a long-running effort to bring the birds back while also drawing attention to the damaged wetlands they depend on. The work has grown into more than a programme to increase stork numbers. It has become a wider restoration effort built around the idea that recovering the bird and recovering its habitat should go together. Today, the project aims to create wetlands of sufficient quality to support at least 100 breeding pairs of white storks in Southern Sweden, giving an old symbol of the region a chance to return.White stork as an ambassador of wetland restoration in Southern SwedenThe disappearance of the white stork was not simply the loss of a single species. According to a study titled ‘The Swedish White Stork Reintroduction Programme,’ the last breeding attempt by a white stork in Sweden failed in 1954. The bird was subsequently declared extinct from the Swedish fauna. The study explains that several factors contributed to the loss, including changes to habitats, increased mortality and a wider decline in European white stork populations. However, the transformation of the landscape was particularly important. Wetlands in southern Sweden had been severely affected by drainage, with the study noting that as much as 90% of them had disappeared from the area. That loss mattered because wetlands provide the kind of feeding grounds storks need. The bird therefore became a highly visible reminder of what had disappeared from the countryside.Since 1989, a reintroduction programme has worked to establish a naturally breeding white stork population in Scania, or Skåne. The programme has involved breeding birds and releasing them, but the wider ambition has always extended beyond that. As the study describes, the white stork has also been used as a flagship species for restoring Sweden’s wetlands. The bird, in other words, became an ambassador for a much larger ecological problem.The main goal of the project, known as ‘White Stork as an Ambassador for Wetlands,’ is to restore wetland habitats capable of supporting a healthy population of white storks. According to the Society for Ecological Restoration(SER), white storks living in areas with high-quality habitat can produce about 40% more young ones that successfully leave the nest than those in poorer habitats. The ideal outcome for storks in the restored landscape is to raise at least two juveniles each year. Over time, this could help create a stable and self-sustaining population rather than one permanently dependent on human intervention.Can a captive-bred population become truly wild againBringing the stork back has not been a straightforward process. Lund University study shows that, by 2012, the project had established 34 free-breeding pairs in Scania. Yet these birds did not necessarily behave like a wild population. Many of the captive-raised birds remained in the region throughout the year because they had become accustomed to being fed in captivity. Their offspring, however, showed an important difference. They were capable of migrating. This created a new possibility for the project. Young birds born within the programme could leave Sweden and, if they later returned as adults to breed, help form a genuinely migratory population.The study reports that changes to the programme had led to approximately 80% of captive-bred juveniles migrating annually since 2010. Their eventual return was identified as an important measure of whether a naturally behaving population could become established. The SER has set an objective that at least 20% of migrating juvenile storks will return to the nesting area as adults to breed. To support that process, the organisations plan to create at least 20 new nesting sites over the course of the project.The future of the stork depends on the landscapeThe white stork’s story in southern Sweden shows why restoring an animal cannot always be separated from restoring the place where it lives. Releasing birds may help rebuild a population, but the long-term future of that population depends on whether the surrounding countryside can provide enough food, nesting opportunities and suitable habitat. Lund University study also documented challenges within the reintroduction programme, including low breeding success and competition for food when birds concentrated around release sites. These difficulties reinforced the importance of spreading the population and improving the wider habitat rather than concentrating conservation efforts in a few locations.The SER’s target of 100 breeding pairs is tied directly to the condition of Southern Sweden’s wetlands. By rebuilding wetlands and creating space for a naturally breeding, migrating population, the project hopes that the white stork will eventually need less help from people. If that happens, the return of the white stork may become one of Southern Sweden’s clearest signs that its lost wetlands are beginning to recover.

articles.title: En 1956, un biólogo colocó una banda metálica en la pata a un albatros: ha seguido su rastro durante 7 décadas, siendo el ave silvestre más longeva del mundo
articles.standfirst: Chandler Robbins hizo historia el 10 de diciembre de 1956 al anillar a un albatros.
articles.summary: Chandler Robbins hizo historia el 10 de diciembre de 1956 al anillar a un albatros.
articles.body: Wisdom, una hembra de albatros de Laysan, ha pasado a la historia por ser el ave más longeva conocida en estado salvaje. Todo empezó por la pericia de un biólogo en diciembre de 1956, cuando Chandler Robbins anilló a una hembra que se encontraba en el atolón de Midway, en pleno océano Pacífico. La identificó con el código Z333, algo que ha ido manteniendo con el paso de los años y de las décadas. Por aquel entonces, Wisdom ya estaba incubando un huevo. Y, claro, este detalle es importante porque los investigadores pudieron determinar que, como tarde, había nacido en 1951. Es decir: seguramente tenga ya alrededor de 75 años o, como mínimo, 74. Es algo extraordinario para un ave marina. ¿Cómo ha conseguido identificarla? Gracias a una anilla metálica que ha permitido su seguimiento durante años. El desgaste del agua salada, la arena y en definitiva el paso del tiempo, ha obligado a que se sustituya. Pero el nombre sigue siendo el mismo. Su historia también ha cambiado lo que los científicos sabían sobre la longevidad de los albatros. De los más de 250.000 ejemplares anillados en Midway desde 1956, el segundo más viejo conocido tiene 52 años. La diferencia con Wisdom es de más de dos décadas. Pero su récord no se limita a la edad. Los investigadores calculan que ha puesto entre 50 y 60 huevos y que ha criado hasta 30 polluelos. En 2024, cuando tenía al menos 73 años, volvió a reproducirse después de varios años sin hacerlo. Tras la desaparición de su pareja habitual, Akeakamai, Wisdom se emparejó con otro macho, identificado como EX25, y consiguió sacar adelante un polluelo en enero de 2025. Wisdom continúa volviendo al atolón cada temporada de cría. Y mientras siga haciéndolo, su propio récord de longevidad seguirá creciendo inevitablemente.

articles.title: A Michigan scientist buried seeds in 20 glass bottles in 1879; 142 years later, some still grew, and the experiment is set to run until 2100
articles.summary: Science News: In 1879, Michigan State University botanist William James Beal buried 20 glass bottles filled with seeds and sand in an effort to answer a deceptively.
articles.body: In 1879, Michigan State University botanist William James Beal buried 20 glass bottles filled with seeds and sand in an effort to answer a deceptively simple question: how long could seeds remain dormant in the soil and still grow when conditions became favourable? According to Michigan State University, more than a century later, the experiment was still producing surprises. In 2021, researchers at Michigan State University unearthed one of the remaining bottles, 142 years after it was buried, and found that some of the seeds could still germinate. The discovery offered a rare glimpse into the extraordinary longevity of seeds and showed why Beal’s experiment remains scientifically relevant more than a century after it began. With bottles still underground, the experiment is scheduled to continue through 2100, making it one of the world’s longest-running scientific experiments.A question from 1879Beal designed the experiment to help farmers understand how long unwanted plants could persist in soil. His concern was practical: if weed seeds could remain dormant for decades, simply removing visible weeds would not necessarily prevent them from returning. To investigate, Beal selected 50 freshly collected seeds from each of 23 plant species. He mixed the seeds with sand and divided them among 20 pint-sized glass bottles. The bottles were left uncorked and buried with their openings pointing downward so rainwater could not collect around the seeds. They were placed on a sandy knoll on the Michigan State campus, creating conditions intended to imitate seeds remaining naturally underground.Testing the buried seedsBeal originally planned to excavate a bottle every five years. During the first decades, researchers repeatedly found that some of the buried seeds could still germinate. The schedule was later changed to preserve the remaining bottles for longer. In 1920, the interval between tests was extended to 10 years. By 1980, it had been increased again, this time to 20 years. That decision transformed the project from a relatively short agricultural experiment into a long-term scientific record of seed longevity.When researchers opened a bottle in 2021, 142 years had passed since Beal buried it. Seeds from the Verbascum group germinated, demonstrating that at least some seeds had remained viable for more than a century. The result was particularly striking because most of the other species included in the original experiment had lost their viability within the first 60 years.DNA revealed another surpriseThe 2021 experiment produced another discovery that Beal could never have anticipated. Researchers used modern genetic testing to identify the plants that emerged from the bottle. The analysis confirmed that the seedlings included moth mullein (Verbascum blattaria) and a hybrid between moth mullein and common mullein (Verbascum thapsus). Beal had recorded that he included only common mullein seeds, suggesting that the hybrid resulted from an accidental mix-up when the bottles were originally prepared. The use of DNA sequencing added a modern layer to a study that began long before genetics became a scientific field.Why the experiment mattersThe Beal Seed Experiment is more than a historical curiosity. Understanding how long seeds can remain viable can help researchers study persistent weeds, manage land restoration and understand how plant species survive in soil seed banks.This information can be particularly useful when restoring former agricultural land. Seeds left behind in soil can potentially emerge many years after cultivation stops, meaning restoration teams need to understand which species may remain dormant and which are unlikely to persist for long periods.The experiment continuesBeal’s original question has still not been completely answered. Researchers cannot simply assume that seeds that failed to germinate are dead; some may remain dormant and require different environmental conditions before they begin growing. Four bottles remain underground. The next bottle is scheduled to be unearthed in 2040, and the final bottles are expected to keep the experiment going until 2100. If seeds germinate again, researchers may consider increasing the interval between future excavations even further.More than 140 years after Beal first buried his bottles, the experiment continues to demonstrate the value of patience in science. What began as an attempt to understand troublesome weeds has become a living record of how long seeds can survive, and a scientific experiment that will outlast generations of researchers.

articles.title: Study: Germany's water deficit growing - even without drought data
articles.summary: The water deficit in Germany and Europe as a whole has worsened in recent months, according to joint studies conducted by Potsdam-based geoscientists working...
articles.body:
Joint studies by Potsdam-based geoscientists, NASA, and DLR reveal worsening water deficit in Germany and Europe, with fears that water reserves may not recover by year-end.

Data up to June did not reflect heatwaves in Germany, indicating that effects of summer heatwaves will only be seen in upcoming months' data, expected in autumn.

Groundwater decline since 2015 is a major factor in long-term water storage decrease in Germany, with heat playing a significant role in reducing water storage capacity.

The water deficit in Germany and Europe as a whole has worsened in recent months, according to joint studies conducted by Potsdam-based geoscientists working with the US space agency NASA and the German Aerospace Center (DLR).

The findings support fears that "water reserves will not recover by the end of the year, even if more rain than usual falls in the autumn," said a spokesman for the Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences (GFZ) in the city by Berlin.

The situation is likely to be even worse because the current data up to June did not reflect the heatwaves in Germany, said the GFZ, which on Thursday published some conclusions from the satellite imaging conducted with partners.

The effects of the heatwaves that wracked Germany and other countries in Europe this summer will only become apparent in the data from the coming months. This data is not expected until autumn.

The researchers are monitoring the total water content on and below the Earth's surface. According to the GFZ, this data allows them to calculate the extent to which water storage capacity is changing.

"Since 2015, we have been seeing increasingly drier conditions in Germany than in the 15 years prior to that," said Annette Eicker, head of the Global Geomonitoring and Gravity Field section at GFZ.

Although the above-average wet year of 2024 brought about some recovery in water storage, this was immediately followed by another sharp decline, according to the institute.

"The decline in groundwater storage accounts for the majority of the long-term decline in water storage in Germany," said Andreas Güntner, hydrology research group leader.

According to the studies, heat, in particular, reduces water storage. A comparison with precipitation data shows no long-term negative trend in precipitation amounts.

However, an increase in potential evaporation due to rising air temperatures is observed - "that is, the amount of water that can be transported from the ground into the atmosphere," said the GFZ spokesman.

articles.title: Sabalenka y el olor a marihuana: la ciencia aclara si puede afectar al rendimiento deportivo
articles.standfirst: La tenista detuvo su partido ante Rakhimova en el US Open: "¿Le importa? Es muy fuerte"
articles.summary: La tenista detuvo su partido ante Rakhimova en el US Open: "¿Le importa? Es muy fuerte"
articles.body: Sabalenka paró su partido contra Rakhimova en el US Open por el fuerte olor a marihuana que sentía. "Alguien está fumando, ¿le importa?... porque es un olor muy fuerte", lamentó durante su encuentro. En rueda de prensa, añadió la siguiente reflexión: "Es un poco difícil soportar ese olor cuando intentas competir al máximo nivel". Este incidente ha protagonizado titulares en todo el mundo. Más allá de la educación en las pistas, estudios científicos aclaran si percibir el olor a marihuana, sustancia psicotrópica, puede afectar al rendimiento mental y deportivo. Un estudio de la Facultad de Medicina de la Universidad Johns Hopkins, en mayo de 2015, publicado en la revista Drug and Alcohol Dependence, examinó dos escenarios. En el primero, se ubicó a los participantes en una habitación ventilada, que no sufrieron los efectos de la droga. Algunos de ellos fumaron la sustancia y otros no. En este último grupo no se detectaron consecuencias negativas: "La exposición en condiciones ventiladas produjo niveles de cannabinoides en sangre mucho más bajos y no produjo efectos sedantes, deterioro del rendimiento ni resultados positivos en la prueba de orina". En el caso de Sabalenka, parece claro aventurar que su rendimiento no se vería afectado por cuestiones médicas, más allá del malestar que le pudiera provocar el olor a marihuana, tal como ella misma denunció durante y después del partido en el US Open. La situación cambia si una persona está sujeta a una exposición indirecta extrema. Es decir, si no la consume de forma directa, pero sí se encuentra en un espacio cerrado donde otros están fumando. En este caso, los efectos el rendimiento físico y mental, y obviamente el deportivo de alto nivel, se verían claramente mermados. El estudio de la Facultad de Medicina de la Universidad Johns Hopkins determinó que, en este escenario, el fumador pasivo sí se vería afectado: "La exposición al humo de cannabis de segunda mano en condiciones sin ventilación produjo niveles detectables de cannabinoides en sangre y orina, aumentos leves de la frecuencia cardíaca y efectos sedantes leves a moderados". La falta de ventilación, en este caso, es clave. En el experimento se ubicó a varios participantes en una habitación sin ella y los resultados fueron contundentes. "En condiciones extremas de falta de ventilación, la exposición al humo de cannabis de segunda mano puede producir niveles detectables de THC en sangre y orina, efectos fisiológicos leves, y un deterioro leve en tareas que requieren capacidad psicomotora".
